sources.title: Sol Plaatje (Q2143151), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-18): the item's English label is the variant spelling 'Sol Plaatjie', description 'South African intellectual, journalist, linguist, politician, translator and writer; founding member and first General Secretary of the South African Native National Congress; regarded as the first Black South African to write a novel in English', instance of human, born 9 October 1876, died 19 June 1932 (two death dates recorded, January and June; the June date is the one used by the sources read), citizen of South Africa, no Korean label. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

South African History Online, 'Solomon Tshekisho Plaatje' biography (read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: mission-school education and private study, work as a Kimberley postman and Mafeking court interpreter during the 1899-1900 siege, proficiency in at least eight languages, founding of the Setswana-English weekly Koranta ea Becoana (1901) with financial backing from Silas Molema and later Tsala ea Becoana and Tsala ea Batho, first secretary-general of the South African Native National Congress (1912), the 1914 deputation to Britain after which he stayed until 1917 and wrote Native Life in South Africa (1916) plus a proverb collection and a Setswana reader, a 1919 meeting with Lloyd George, a North American trip from 1920, Mhudi (1930) and Setswana Shakespeare translations, the 1972 publication of his Mafeking diary. Notes that claims of his attending pan-African congresses are unsupported. Encyclopaedic institutional biography; dates differ slightly from other sources.

Lucien van der Walt, 'Plaatje, Solomon Tshekisho (1876-1932)', in the International Encyclopaedia of Revolution and Protest (Blackwell, 2009; online edition, read in full). Scholarly entry from a labour-history perspective: three years of formal schooling, assistant teacher at 15, work as a Kimberley postman and Mafeking clerk and interpreter, the Koranta ea Becoana paper (1902-08), his role in forming the South African Native Press Association (1903), work as a mine labour contractor from 1909, tours of the Orange Free State and Cape to document the effects of the 1913 Land Act that became Native Life in South Africa, his staying on in Britain at his own expense after the 1914 deputation and translating Julius Caesar into Setswana in 1917, declining the SANNC presidency, work in sound recording and film in 1922, his moderate political style and his view of the syndicalists as lamentable; says that by the 1920s he was no longer an important leader.

Neil Parsons, introduction to the electronic text of Sol Plaatje's 'Native Life in South Africa' (University of Botswana History Department; read in full). Historian's 1998 introduction: Plaatje's quick rise through the Cape civil service examinations, his Mafeking siege diary and its early prose experimentation, the unpublished 1908-09 booklet 'Sekgoma, the Black Dreyfus', his decision to stay in England to fight the Land Act through writing and lecturing, collaboration with Professor Daniel Jones on Setswana, a 1919 meeting with Lloyd George, a 1921 American lecture tour paid for by selling about 18,000 copies of a booklet, a turning from politics to literature after the early 1920s, and the later publication of Mhudi in a version Parsons calls somewhat bowdlerized. Admiring but frames his political efforts as largely unsuccessful.

Brian Willan, 'What Other Devils? The Texts of Sol T. Plaatje's Mhudi Revisited', Journal of Southern African Studies (2015; author PDF, read in the sections on Mhudi's publication). Archival scholarship by Plaatje's biographer: Mhudi was finished in London by July 1920, Plaatje spent 18 months in North America trying without success to place it with Macmillan, Harper, Scribner's and Harcourt, Allen and Unwin offered to publish in 1922 on a 75-pound subsidy he could not raise, other London publishers also failed, and in November 1929 he approached the Lovedale Press (which turned down his Setswana Shakespeare translations but accepted Mhudi); his handwritten changes to the typescript fit a habit of repeated redrafting and the novel was contracted in March 1930 at a price he proposed. Argues against the view that the missionary press censored him. The same author as the standard biography.

Daniel Jones, 'The Phonetic Structure of the Sechuana Language' (paper read to the Philological Society, 4 May 1917; Transactions of the Philological Society; read in full from the open-access copy). Primary contemporary account by his collaborator: states that his work on the language was done in collaboration with Mr S. T. Plaatje, a Rolong native of Mafeking, cites Plaatje's 'Sechuana Proverbs' (1916) for the shortcomings of the five conventional orthographies and gives the pronunciation of his surname, which Jones writes as 'plaki' and says is often pronounced 'placi'. Short technical paper; evidence of collaboration, not of character.

'Solomon Tshekisho Plaatje', Encyclopedia of World Biography (Gale, reproduced on Encyclopedia.com; read in full). Short reference entry: multilingual interpreter, founder of the first Tswana newspaper, secretary general of the SANNC, evidence-gathering tour of the Orange Free State, 1914 deputation, books of 1915-16 written in Britain, the Setswana Shakespeare translations of 1930 and 1937, and the novel Mhudi, rejected by several publishers before Lovedale printed it in 1930; reads Mhudi as seeking to counter European misconceptions about African women and to point to similarities between Barolong and Boer aspirations. Brief and literary-minded; its dates for his birth and some publications differ from the other sources.

Sol T. Plaatje, 'Native Life in South Africa, Before and Since the European War and the Boer Rebellion' (London: P. S. King and Son, 1916; the chapter 'Who is the Author?' read in the Digital Library of India scan on the Internet Archive, the prologue in the University of Botswana electronic text). SELF-AUTHORED PRIMARY TEXT, so used with caution: in the prologue he says the information comes from his own inquiry in the Transvaal, Orange Free State and Cape, that he stopped his Free State inquiry in September 1913 when his money ran out, and that friends paid for part of a six-week Cape tour; the front chapter reprints two testimonials, a 1906 note from the Duke of Connaught and a 1910 Pretoria News editorial describing his schooling, private study and results in the civil service examinations. The testimonials were chosen for the book itself.

persistence.rationale: [src_plaatje_willan, src_plaatje_saho, src_plaatje_vdw, src_plaatje_parsons | 1914-1930 | scholarly article, reference biography, encyclopaedia entry, historian's introduction] After his novel Mhudi was finished in 1920 he spent 18 months in North America trying to place it with Macmillan, Harper, Scribner's and Harcourt, all of which declined; in 1922 Allen and Unwin offered to publish if he found a 75-pound subsidy he could not raise; he returned in 1923 with it unpublished and approached the Lovedale Press in 1929, which printed it in 1930. Earlier, after the failed 1914 deputation he stayed in Britain until 1917 at his own expense to continue the campaign, and returned in 1919. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION: lowered from 78 / 0.66 because the Mhudi rejections rest on one scholar and the Britain episode on summaries drawn from one biography.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_plaatje_saho, src_plaatje_vdw, src_plaatje_parsons, src_plaatje_nativelife | 1901-1921 | reference biography, encyclopaedia entry, historian's introduction, self-authored book] He started the first Setswana-English weekly in 1901-02 with a chief's backing and later founded further papers in Kimberley, took a role in forming a native press association in 1903, in 1913 set out on private inquiry tours of the Free State and Cape to document the Land Act evictions (his own prologue says friends paid), and chose to stay in England after the deputation left in order to keep fighting by writing and lecturing. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION: lowered from 78 / 0.66 because the field tours rest on his own prologue and the press founding on reference summaries of one biography.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_plaatje_saho, src_plaatje_parsons, src_plaatje_vdw, src_plaatje_nativelife | 1913-1930 | reference biography, historian's introduction, encyclopaedia entry, self-authored book] Over about two decades he repeatedly put his own time and money into getting the position of Black South Africans before a wider public: the evidence-gathering tours and Native Life in South Africa (1916), three years in Britain, an 18-month North American trip, reporting on Parliament and lobbying in Cape Town after 1923, a role in the 1930 deputation on the pass laws, and prolific letters to the press. The behaviour is documented across four sources, though outcomes were mostly unsuccessful.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_plaatje_parsons, src_plaatje_saho, src_plaatje_nativelife | 1913-1921 | historian's introduction, reference biography, self-authored book] Parsons says he paid his way through a 1921 American lecture tour by publishing and selling about 18,000 copies of a booklet at 25 cents; the reference biography adds that while in Britain he worked as a language assistant at London University; his own prologue says he finished his 1913 inquiry with help from friends who paid fares. The booklet sale rests on one historian's sentence. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION: lowered from 70 / 0.54 and downgraded to inference because the strongest instance rests on a single historian's sentence and the rest on his own account.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_plaatje_saho, src_plaatje_vdw, src_plaatje_parsons, src_plaatje_ewb | 1894-1932 | reference biography, encyclopaedia entry, historian's introduction, encyclopaedia entry] Sources describe sustained work in court interpreting and clerking, newspaper editing, mine labour contracting, organising, Setswana phonetics and proverb collection with a University of London phonetician, a novel, Shakespeare translation into Setswana and, in 1922, sound recording and film production. Each strand produced output, but the four summaries draw on the same biography. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION: lowered from 74 / 0.64 because the reference entries are derivative of one underlying biography.

adaptability.rationale: [src_plaatje_saho, src_plaatje_parsons, src_plaatje_vdw | 1914-1930 | reference biography, historian's introduction, encyclopaedia entry] When the 1914 deputation failed he changed method from delegation to writing, lecturing and language work in Britain; after the 1919 delegation he moved to a North American lecture tour and publishing; after 1923 he combined journalism and lobbying with the Joint Council movement and, on Parsons's reading, turned to literature. The sources do not agree on how far he left politics. SELF-CALIBRATION: lowered from 66 / 0.50 and downgraded to inference because the three accounts disagree on his later course.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_plaatje_nativelife, src_plaatje_vdw, src_plaatje_jones, src_plaatje_parsons | 1890s-1917 | self-authored book with printed testimonials, encyclopaedia entry, collaborator's paper, historian's introduction] A 1910 newspaper tribute printed in his book says that while a postman he studied languages in his spare time and headed the Cape civil service examination lists in typewriting, Dutch and native languages; later he compiled Setswana proverbs with European equivalents and worked with Daniel Jones on the language's sounds (Jones credits the collaboration); sources agree he used about eight languages. SELF-CALIBRATION: lowered from 70 / 0.56 because the examination results come from a testimonial that his own book chose to print.

collaboration.rationale: [src_plaatje_jones, src_plaatje_parsons | 1915-1917 | collaborator's paper, historian's introduction] Jones writes in 1917 that his work on the Setswana language was done in collaboration with Plaatje, and Parsons says the 1916 Sechuana Reader was co-authored with Jones. This is one documented partnership of short duration; his work within congress delegations is organisational and is not used here. SELF-CALIBRATION: lowered from 60 / 0.46 because it rests on one partnership.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_plaatje_parsons, src_plaatje_ewb, src_plaatje_willan | 1900-1930 | historian's introduction, encyclopaedia entry, scholarly article] Parsons describes his siege diary as early prose experimentation that mixes languages and idioms; the encyclopaedia entry reads Mhudi as a deliberate retelling of 1830s history from the Barolong side that names the story for its heroine; Willan documents repeated redrafting of the novel. These are interpretive literary readings by later writers, not first-hand evidence of how he generated ideas.

portrait.source: Half-tone photographic plate captioned 'The Author. (Photo by Wakefield, Ealing, W.)' showing Plaatje seated at a desk writing, facing the title page of 'Native Life in South Africa, Before and Since the European War and the Boer Rebellion, by Sol. T. Plaatje' (London: P. S. King and Son; first edition May 1916, later printings to 1921; the scanned copy is an undated P. S. King printing with 24 chapters and an epilogue, so the exact printing is not identified). Taken from the Digital Library of India scan of the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration library copy on the Internet Archive (item in.ernet.dli.2015.236312, 358 pages, bitonal 600 ppi scan, opened and checked page 5); the plate was cropped to the printed photograph and reduced about 2.4 times to 837 x 1056 pixels (downscaled only, never upscaled). The scan renders the half-tone in two tones only, so the face is coarse and the right eye is blown out; the likeness is recognisable in profile but of low visual quality.
portrait.license: Public domain in the United States: a photograph published in London in 1916 or the following years in a book (published before 1931). Digital Library of India item metadata (dc.rights) states 'Out_of_copyright'. The photographer is the studio 'Wakefield, Ealing' (individual not identified, death date unknown), so the United Kingdom term was not independently resolved; for a photograph published more than a century ago by a commercial studio this is flagged for lead review rather than relied on.
portrait.attribution: Photo by Wakefield, Ealing (studio), plate in Sol T. Plaatje, Native Life in South Africa (London: P. S. King and Son, 1916); scan: Digital Library of India / Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration library, via the Internet Archive
portrait.creator: Wakefield, Ealing (photographic studio)
portrait.date: 1916 (book printing; photograph undated, taken during his stay in London 1914-1917)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (Stage B) / lead FAILED, REPLACEMENT used: the Stage B lead 'Sol Plaatje 002.jpg' (Commons, 204 x 228 pixels, claimed 'from his 1915 book', c.1900) was checked and rejected: it is a different, much earlier studio photograph of a young Plaatje in a bow tie that is NOT among the plates of Native Life in South Africa (the scan has only 'The Author' at a desk and a portrait of Mrs Plaatje), so its book provenance claim is unsupported, the publication year is also wrong (first edition May 1916, per the Cambridge editions chapter), and the file is tiny. REPLACEMENT: the captioned plate 'The Author (Photo by Wakefield, Ealing, W.)' in the Digital Library of India scan of Native Life in South Africa (P. S. King, London; Internet Archive item in.ernet.dli.2015.236312, opened, page 5) facing a title page that names Sol. T. Plaatje as author; cropped and downscaled 2.4 times from a 2768 x 4088 bitonal scan to 837 x 1056, not upscaled. HOLDER RECORD: the Internet Archive/Digital Library of India metadata says dc.rights Out_of_copyright (source library: Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration, Mussoorie); the DLI handle site itself was unreachable (connection failed) and the University of Fort Hare repository copy of the 1916 edition (also unreachable, connection refused) could not be checked. The printing of the scanned copy is not identified (first edition May 1916, later printings 1916-1921 per the Cambridge editions chapter, which does not state whether the first edition carried this plate). QUALITY AND RIGHTS CAVEATS FOR LEAD: (1) the scan is a coarse two-tone half-tone: face and right eye are degraded, so the portrait is a recognisable but low-quality likeness; Mhudi (1930) has no author portrait (title page checked via Commons), and no better-quality pre-1931 scan was found in one bounded retry (Wikimedia upload hosts returned HTTP 429 for some file downloads; the 1916 Fort Hare scan was unreachable). (2) Rights: PD in the US as a pre-1931 publication; the photographer is the studio 'Wakefield, Ealing' and the UK term for that studio's work was not resolved. Wikimedia 'Sol Plaatje (centre) in Cradle of the World 1923' is a group film still, not a portrait, and ANC1914.jpg is a delegation group photograph; neither used. IDENTITY: QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-18) Q2143151, label 'Sol Plaatjie' (variant spelling; canonicalName follows the standard 'Sol Plaatje' used by SAHO, the Sol Plaatje University and Commons), description as in the source card, human, born 9 October 1876, died 19 June 1932 (a second January death date is recorded and not used); no Korean label. REGION sub_saharan_africa (precedents: Winnie Madikizela-Mandela, Kwame Nkrumah); ERA 20th_century (Native Life 1916, Mhudi 1930); nationality ZA. KOREAN NAME 솔 플라치 is a standard transliteration (English pronunciation 'PLAH-chee', Jones 1917 gives 'plaki, often placi'); no established Korean name exists (Korean Wikipedia's ANC article spells him 솔 플랏케, which is not standard) - see handback koreanNameFlags. COMPOSITION FLAG FOR LEAD: Plaatje is a journalist, linguist, novelist and translator as well as the first secretary-general of the SANNC; the profile scores only documented behaviour (publishing, persistence, language work, campaigning travel) and does not score political ideology or party-political positions; the SANNC role and the 1913 Land Act campaign are described in editorial as context; lead may weigh this against the zero-politics composition rule. SOURCES READ: SAHO biography, van der Walt encyclopaedia entry, Parsons introduction (University of Botswana e-text), Willan 2015 JSAS article (Mhudi publication sections), Jones 1917 Philological Society paper, Encyclopedia of World Biography entry, Native Life 'Who is the Author?' chapter (via DLI scan OCR) and prologue (e-text). NOT OPENED: Willan's biographies (1984 and 2018), Mafeking diary, Mhudi text, Cambridge book chapters other than the editions chapter (read for dating only), Willan's SOAS thesis (host unreachable), Wikipedia. CONFLICTS: Koranta ea Becoana founded 1901 (SAHO, EWB) or 1902 (van der Walt); death date January vs June 1932; whether he left politics after the early 1920s (Parsons, EWB) or kept lobbying (SAHO, van der Walt); Parsons gives five Shakespeare translations, SAHO four, EWB two dated. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: src_plaatje_saho. Nine rows initially; seven lowered (four for source-family concentration, three in self-calibration); no row raised. Non-self behavioural sources: Willan 2015 (archival scholarship), Jones 1917 (collaborator), Parsons, van der Walt, SAHO; note most reference sources derive from one biographer's work.
